_comment: Useful phrases (Redemittel) by speech act: agreeing, disagreeing, doubting, comforting … Each set is a flashcard deck (/vocabulary/phrases/<id>) and a row under the phrases on /pronunciation. The key `de` holds the Portuguese phrase that is practised (the key name is history, see docs/content-plan.md §1.4); `en` is the English meaning, with a short usage note where it helps. Every phrase has `variety` (pt-PT), and `ptBR` where Brazilian usage differs (nothing is shown for it until a Brazil mode exists). Forms of address follow Portugal: tu between friends and in the informal sets, o senhor / a senhora (verb in the 3rd person) with strangers, in services and at work; você is avoided. Phrase order matters: the beginner path refers to phrases as redemittel:<set>#<index>. Translations live in src/data/redemittel-i18n/<lang>.json, keyed by the Portuguese phrase: machine drafts until a native speaker has read them (reviewed: false). Audio: scripts/generate-satz-audio.mjs → public/audio/redemittel/<slug>.mp3 (none yet for the Portuguese phrases).

phrases.en: You're right. (To someone you call o senhor / a senhora: Tem razão.)
I completely agree.
Exactly!
I agree with you.
I think so too.
That's exactly what I think.
That sounds like a good idea. (The pronoun comes after the verb in Portugal: parece-me.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil the pronoun usually comes before the verb in speech: Me parece uma boa ideia.

phrases.en: OK, agreed. Está bem is the everyday “OK” in Portugal.

ptBR.note: In Brazil people say Tá bom, combinado, or Beleza in informal speech.

phrases.de: Eu vejo isso de outra maneira.
phrases.en: I see it differently.
I don't agree.
That's not quite right.
I'm sorry, but I disagree. A polite way to say no. (With o senhor: Desculpe.)
I don't think that's true. (After não acho que comes the subjunctive: seja.)
I don't think so.
Yes, but … You agree a little, then add your point.
No way! (informal)
I'm not so sure about that. (A woman says: certa.)
Do you really think so?

phrases.de: Não sei, não tenho a certeza.
phrases.en: I don't know, I'm not sure. In Portugal you “have” certainty: ter a certeza.

ptBR.note: In Brazil you hear Não sei, não tenho certeza, usually without the article.

phrases.de: Tens a certeza de que é assim?
phrases.en: Are you sure it's like that?

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Você tem certeza de que é assim? (no article, and você).
ptBR.form: Você tem certeza de que é assim?

phrases.en: I find that hard to believe.

ptBR.note: In Brazil the pronoun comes first: Me custa acreditar, or more often É difícil acreditar.

phrases.en: Hmm, I have my doubts.
Are you sure? (To o senhor / a senhora: Tem a certeza?)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Você tem certeza? (no article).

phrases.en: I doubt it.
I'm so sorry. Used for bad news; Sinto muito is also common.
Hang in there! Keep going!
It'll all go well. (Literally: everything will run well.)
Don't worry. (With o senhor: Não se preocupe.)

phrases.de: Estou aqui para o que precisares.
phrases.en: I'm here for whatever you need.
It's not that bad. Careful: with a real problem it can sound dismissive.
You can do it!

ptBR.note: In Brazil you usually say Você consegue!, with você.

phrases.de: Posso fazer alguma coisa por ti?
phrases.en: Is there anything I can do for you? (With o senhor: por si.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Posso fazer alguma coisa por você? (por ti is rare).
ptBR.form: Posso fazer alguma coisa por você?

phrases.en: My view is that …

ptBR.note: Brazilian speech often drops the article: Minha opinião é que …

phrases.en: I think that … The easiest way to give your opinion.
In my opinion, …
It seems to me that …

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Me parece que … (pronoun before the verb).

phrases.de: Para mim, o importante é que …
phrases.en: What matters to me is that … (Often followed by the subjunctive.)
To be honest, … (A woman says: sincera.)
That seems fine to me.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Me parece bom, or Acho bom.

phrases.en: And what do you think? (To o senhor / a senhora: E o senhor, o que acha?)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: E você, o que acha? (você, and the 3rd person).

phrases.en: Sorry? / Pardon? You didn't hear what someone said. Desculpe? works too.
Could you say that again, please? (With tu: Podes repetir?)

phrases.de: Pode falar mais devagar, por favor?
phrases.en: Could you speak more slowly, please?
What does that mean?
Sorry, I didn't understand that. Percebi is the everyday verb in Portugal.

ptBR.note: In Brazil entender is more usual: Desculpe, não entendi.

phrases.en: How do you spell that?
Do you mean that …? You check that you have understood.
Could you give me an example?

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Pode me dar um exemplo? (pronoun before the infinitive).

phrases.en: Could you help me, please? A polite way to ask.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Pode me ajudar, por favor? (pronoun before the infinitive).

phrases.en: Have you got a minute? (With tu: Tens um minuto?)

phrases.de: Podes passar-me o sal, por favor?
phrases.en: Could you pass me the salt, please?

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Pode me passar o sal, por favor? (você; pronoun first).
ptBR.form: Pode me passar o sal, por favor?

phrases.en: Could I ask you a favour? (With tu: Posso pedir-te um favor?)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Posso te pedir um favor? (pronoun before the verb).

phrases.en: Sorry to bother you. Say this before you interrupt someone.
Could you show me?

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Pode me mostrar? (pronoun before the infinitive).

phrases.en: I need some help.
Would that be possible?
Sorry! For a small mistake, or when you bump into someone. (With o senhor: Desculpe!)
I'm really sorry. A fuller, polite apology.
I didn't mean it like that.
Sorry I'm late. (With o senhor: Desculpe o atraso.)
That was my fault.
No problem. An answer to an apology: it's OK.

ptBR.note: In Brazil you also hear Tudo bem or Sem problema as the answer.

phrases.en: It doesn't matter. An answer to an apology: forget it.
It could happen to anyone. An answer to an apology.
Thank you very much! A woman says: Muito obrigada! (obrigado/obrigada agrees with the speaker.)
Thanks, that's very kind of you. (To a woman: simpática; to o senhor: é muito simpático.)
Thank you so much for your help. (With o senhor: pela sua ajuda.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil people say Obrigado pela sua ajuda (você), seldom pela tua.

phrases.en: How kind of you! For a small gift or a kind gesture.
You're welcome! An answer to thank you.
It was my pleasure. An answer to thank you.
Don't mention it. An answer to thank you.

ptBR.note: In Brazil the usual answer is Imagina or Por nada; Não tem de quê is rarer.

phrases.en: I really appreciate it. (With o senhor: Agradeço-lhe imenso.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Agradeço muito, or Eu te agradeço muito (proclisis).

phrases.en: How about going by metro? Que tal + personal infinitive (irmos, vermos, fazermos) is typical of Portugal.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Que tal a gente ir de metrô? (a gente, and metrô).
ptBR.form: Que tal a gente ir de metrô?

phrases.en: Shall we go out for a meal?

phrases.de: Proponho que nos encontremos às oito.
phrases.en: I suggest that we meet at eight. (Followed by the subjunctive: encontremos.)
Do you fancy going to the cinema? Apetecer takes the person as indirect object: apetece-me, apetece-te.

ptBR.note: In Brazil people say Você quer ir ao cinema? or Está a fim de ir ao cinema?

phrases.en: Good idea, let's do that! A yes to a suggestion.
Sorry, I can't make it that day. A no to a suggestion.
Maybe another time.
Does Saturday suit you? Dar jeito = to be convenient. (With o senhor: dá-lhe jeito.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: O sábado fica bom para você? or Sábado dá para você?
ptBR.form: O sábado fica bom para você?

phrases.en: Congratulations! For an exam, a new job, a baby, and also on a birthday.
Happy birthday! Parabéns! is just as common.
Good luck!
Good luck with your exam!

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Boa sorte na prova! (prova is the usual word for an exam).

phrases.en: Get well soon! To someone who is ill.
Have a nice weekend! Said on Friday.
Merry Christmas! Boas Festas! covers Christmas and New Year.
I'm so happy for you!

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Fico tão feliz por você! (feliz and você).

phrases.en: Good morning! Used until about midday or lunch; after that: Boa tarde!
Nice to meet you. Muito prazer is the usual short form. (With o senhor: conhecê-lo; a woman: conhecê-la.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Prazer em te conhecer (proclisis, te).

phrases.en: How are you? Answer: Tudo bem, obrigado. E tu? (A woman says: obrigada.)
Long time no see! (informal)
See you tomorrow!
Goodbye! Also Até logo! (see you later) and Até já! (see you in a moment).

ptBR.note: In Brazil Tchau is the everyday goodbye; Adeus sounds final.

phrases.en: Take care! A friendly goodbye.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Se cuida! (pronoun before the verb).

phrases.en: Have a good day! (With o senhor: Que tenha um bom dia!)
In the picture I can see … The easiest way to start. Foto is the short form.

phrases.de: A fotografia mostra uma família a comer.
phrases.en: The picture shows a family having a meal. You say what it is about. (a comer = eating: estar a + infinitive.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil: A foto mostra uma família comendo (gerund, no a + infinitive).
ptBR.form: A foto mostra uma família comendo.

phrases.en: In the foreground you can see …

ptBR.note: In Brazil: Em primeiro plano se vê … (se before the verb).

phrases.en: In the background there's a park.

ptBR.note: In Brazil people say Ao fundo tem um parque (tem for há in speech).

phrases.en: In the middle there's a table.

ptBR.note: In Brazil people say No centro tem uma mesa (tem for há in speech).

phrases.de: À esquerda há uma jovem sentada.
phrases.en: On the left there's a young woman sitting down.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: À esquerda tem uma jovem sentada (tem for há in speech).
ptBR.form: À esquerda tem uma jovem sentada.

phrases.de: No canto superior direito há uma janela.
phrases.en: In the top right-hand corner there's a window.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: No canto superior direito tem uma janela (tem for há in speech).
ptBR.form: No canto superior direito tem uma janela.

phrases.de: Provavelmente as pessoas estão de férias.
phrases.en: The people are probably on holiday. A guess about the situation.

phrases.de: Acho que é uma festa de anos.
phrases.en: I think it's a birthday party. A guess about the situation. Festa de aniversário is the longer form.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: festa de aniversário; festa de anos is not used.
ptBR.form: Acho que é uma festa de aniversário.

phrases.en: It looks as if everyone is happy.
The atmosphere is relaxed.

phrases.de: A fotografia faz-me lembrar a minha infância.
phrases.en: The picture reminds me of my childhood. You connect it with your own life.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: A foto me lembra a minha infância, or me faz lembrar (pronoun first).
ptBR.form: A foto me lembra a minha infância.

phrases.de: A bola está dentro da caixa.
phrases.en: The ball is in the box.

phrases.de: A bola está em cima da caixa.
phrases.en: The ball is on the box.

phrases.de: A bola está debaixo da mesa.
phrases.en: The ball is under the table.

phrases.de: O candeeiro está pendurado por cima da mesa.
phrases.en: The lamp is hanging above the table. (Por cima de = above; em cima de = on top of.)

ptBR.note: In Brazil a hanging lamp is a luminária or lustre; candeeiro is not used.
ptBR.form: A luminária está pendurada por cima da mesa.

phrases.de: A bola está ao lado da caixa.
phrases.en: The ball is next to the box.

phrases.de: A bola está à frente da caixa.
phrases.en: The ball is in front of the box.

ptBR.note: In Brazil na frente da caixa is more common than à frente da caixa.
ptBR.form: A bola está na frente da caixa.

phrases.de: A bola está atrás da caixa.
phrases.en: The ball is behind the box.

phrases.de: A bola está entre as caixas.
phrases.en: The ball is between the boxes.
The picture is on the wall. (Em covers “in”, “on” and “at”: na = em + a.)
